analysis.one_liner: Suspends federal prevailing-wage requirements for construction contracts in areas hit by major disasters.
analysis.headline: A bill to let federal contractors pay below prevailing wages on disaster cleanup died in committee without a vote, after 41 House Republicans cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction to pay workers the local prevailing wage, typically union-scale rates. This bill would suspend that rule for one year anywhere the President declares a major disaster, letting contractors on disaster cleanup and rebuilding pay whatever the market allows. It was introduced just after Hurricane Katrina, when Congress was weighing how to pay for Gulf Coast reconstruction. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal disaster-reconstruction contractors gain the most: they could win government-funded cleanup and rebuilding work while paying workers less than the prevailing wage, widening their margins on every contract. Taxpayers could see some savings if lower labor costs cut bid prices, though contractors are not required to pass savings on.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Davis-Bacon Act so that its wage-rate requirements do not apply in any area the President declares a major disaster, for one year from the declaration.
Contractors on federally funded disaster work could then pay market wages rather than the local prevailing rates Davis-Bacon requires, reducing their labor costs on government contracts.
The bill was introduced days after Hurricane Katrina, when federal money for Gulf Coast cleanup and rebuilding was the dominant construction-contracting opportunity in the country.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on disaster rebuilding pay the cost: in the areas where the suspension applies, their pay would drop from the prevailing wage to whatever contractors offer, at exactly the moment when a disaster has destroyed local housing and driven up living costs. The building-trades unions that administer and rely on the prevailing-wage system also lose ground.

drawbacks.text: In a declared disaster area, the bill removes the prevailing-wage floor for federal contracts, so workers doing the rebuilding would be paid less while local living costs spike after the disaster.

Lower pay can make it harder to attract skilled tradespeople to disaster zones, potentially slowing reconstruction or lowering its quality; the bill sets no requirement that contractor savings be passed to taxpayers.

Supporters' good-faith case is that Davis-Bacon raises the federal cost of disaster response and can delay urgent cleanup, and that waiving it lets more contractors bid and work start sooner; the bill takes the broadest possible approach, suspending the wage rule for a full year and in every declared disaster nationwide rather than targeting genuine emergencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to taxpayers are indirect and speculative, since contractors would keep whatever margin lower wages produce, while the cost to workers is direct and concentrated on people rebuilding after a disaster, when they are most vulnerable. Waiving wage rules for a short emergency window is a defensible idea in principle, but a blanket one-year suspension in every declared disaster area nationwide goes well beyond the emergency-clearing work where the argument is strongest.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to its workforce protections subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no action.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Flake introduced the bill on September 7, 2005, with 29 original cosponsors, days after Hurricane Katrina.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction.
About a month later, on October 12, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained with no further action.
The bill accumulated 41 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers and the building-trades unions are better off, because the prevailing-wage floor on federal disaster contracts stayed intact. Contractors who hoped to bid on disaster rebuilding at below-prevailing labor costs lost the opportunity, at least through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Jeff Flake
for.role: Sponsor, House Freedom-style conservative Republican from Arizona
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage rules in disaster areas.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill was referred to the Workforce Protections subcommittee and died there.

against.name: John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a markup or floor action during the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill also never advanced in a committee chaired by a Republican, so the opposition that mattered was inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have let them cut labor costs on government-funded disaster work by paying below prevailing wages; because it died, they keep paying Davis-Bacon rates. Their gain under the bill would have come directly out of workers' pay on public contracts.

industries.industry: Building-trades unions and union-scale construction labor
industries.note: Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage rules are the standard these workers and unions rely on for federally funded work; the bill would have removed that floor in every declared disaster area for a year, cutting union-scale pay on disaster rebuilding.
